This paper introduces a unified benchmarking framework, STEP, to evaluate Spiking Transformers across architectures, datasets, and tasks,  analyze modules, sequence, encoding, efficiency, and accuracy, and provide design insights.

The main strengths of this paper are:

- consistent practices of Spiking Transformers' evaluation  (Reviewer xdDS, YdQb, QuX2)
- comprehensive experiments and ablation studies  (Reviewer xdDS, gQSs, YdQb, QuX2)
- interesting analysis with valuable insights  (Reviewer xdDS, YdQb, QuX2)


The main weaknesses of this paper are:
- the needs of more discussion/evaluations on variants/datasets/modules analysis of Spiking Transformer,  other architectures like spiking CNN (Reviewer xdDS, gQSs, YdQb, QuX2)
- the needs of discussion on real-world hardware or deployment like neuromorphic chips (Reviewer xdDS,gQSs,QuX2)
- the lack of confidence intervals or standard deviation of results (Reviewer xdDS)
- the needs of clarification like reproduction, and representative models (Reviewer YdQb)


During the rebuttal phase, the authors have provided the necessary discussions and more experiments. All concerns have been addressed. Overall, this paper received a consistent positive recommendation, 3 accept and 1 borderline accept from the reviewers. After reading the review, discussion, and rebuttal, the AC agrees with its unified benchmarking framework, comprehensive experiments, and ablation studies, and valuable insights. In this case, the AC recommends an Accept.

We’re grateful for your thoughtful feedback and your consideration in reevaluating your score. As we mentioned in our rebuttal, all suggested revisions will be carefully incorporated into the final camera-ready version to ensure the highest quality. If you have any further thoughts or recommendations, we’d be glad to hear them.

Thank you for carefully reading our work. We sincerely appreciate both your positive feedback and the critical questions you raised.

## Response to Scope of the Framework (General SNN Support)
We fully agree that developing a unified benchmarking framework for general SNNs is of great significance. However, Spiking Transformer represents a rapidly evolving subfield within the SNN community, characterized by architectural challenges that are fundamentally distinct from traditional convolution-based SNNs—such as the use of spiking attention mechanisms, high memory access demands, and hybrid computation paradigms. Despite growing research interest, this area still lacks a systematic and standardized benchmarking foundation. Therefore, STEP is designed to **first address this specific gap**.
It is important to emphasize that STEP adopts **a highly modular and extensible architecture**, encompassing components such as input encoding, spiking neuron models, and backend interfaces. This ensures natural generalizability across architectures. To demonstrate this, we have already integrated several representative non-Transformer models into STEP—including CNN-based (ResNet19, VGG), RNN-based, and SSM-based architectures—and reproduced their results across tasks like image classification, event recognition, and audio sequence classification. These efforts showcase STEP’s model-agnostic flexibility and rapid adaptability.
**Experiments on More SNN Models with STEP**
| Model      | Dataset| Task| Step |Acc@1 | Batch-Size | Epoch|
|:------------:|:------:|:-----:|:---:|:----:|:------------:|:--------------:|
| ResNet19_SNN | CIFAR10| cls |4|94.83      | 128       | 400       |
| VGG_SNN      | CIFAR10| cls |4| 93.39      | 128       | 400      |
|       | | ||      |      |   |
| SpikingSSM[1]      | sCIFAR10| sequence_cls |4| 87.7      | 50       | 200      |
|       | | ||      |      |   |
| RNN_SNN[2]      | DVS_Gesture| dvs_cls |10| 97.34      | 32      | 200      |
| RNN_SNN[2]      |SHD| dvs_audio_cls |250| 86.83     | 32      | 200      |
|       | | ||      |      |   |

Looking ahead, we plan to extend STEP to support broader SNN architectures, with the goal of evolving STEP into a unified benchmarking platform that serves the entire SNN research community.




## Response to Fairness of Evaluation Standards and Code Accessibility
**Ensuring fair and reproducible comparisons is a core design principle of STEP**. To this end, all models in our benchmark are re-implemented or adapted to follow unified training configurations, data augmentation strategies, optimizers, learning schedules, and evaluation metrics. We fix the random seed and strictly avoid any form of cherry-picking. Although this may lead to discrepancies compared to the original papers—which often use different training scripts and tuning heuristics—we believe this normalization is essential for revealing the true relative performance of competing designs.
Regarding dataset and code accessibility, we would like to emphasize that STEP currently does not introduce new datasets; instead, **all datasets used are publicly available**. Our framework includes **standardized preprocessing and data augmentation pipelines** for each dataset, and all training and evaluation scripts are **fully open-sourced** on GitHub. To further improve reproducibility, we have released a detailed user manual and uploaded all model checkpoints and log files to the cloud. Researchers can directly download and run our models with minimal setup. We hope this resolves any concerns about the fairness and accessibility of our benchmarking setup.


## Response to Unified Energy Estimation
Thank you for acknowledging the importance of a unified energy estimation model. We agree that accurate modeling depends on assumptions about hardware factors such as memory access costs and temporal sparsity. To address this, we carefully based our estimation **on well-established energy models from prior neuromorphic hardware literature**, explicitly accounting for both compute and memory access components—the latter of which is often ignored in previous spiking model evaluations.
We also want to stress that there is currently no neuromorphic hardware capable of deploying Spiking Transformers at scale, as such models involve non-event-driven operations and large memory footprints. While hardware deployment would certainly provide direct validation, the incompatibility and scaling challenges (e.g., requiring hundreds of Loihi chips for a single model) make this infeasible for fair cross-model comparison. As a result, **our simulation-based estimation is not only justified but necessary, and we see it as a foundation for future efforts once hardware matures to support such architectures**.

Thank you for carefully reviewing our work and for your thoughtful and targeted feedback. 

## Response to Model Selection
Thanks again for your suggestions. Spiking Transformer has made significant progress and advancements, and recently, several new versions of Spiking Transformer have emerged. However, replicating all versions of Spiking Transformer and achieving results on all datasets is a massive undertaking that requires substantial computational and time costs.

In CIFAR10/100 and subsequent component-level work, we primarily selected three works: Spikformer , SDT, and Spikformer+SEMM. Spikformer, as **the first SNN to introduce the attention mechanism**, laid the foundation for the Spiking Transformer field[1]. SDT **ensures a Spike-Driven architecture** and reduces the attention complexity to $O(ND)$[2]. SEMM was the **first to introduce the MoE system** into Spiking Transformer. These three works are crucial to the development of Spiking Transformer[3]. Since the experiments on ImageNet require high computational costs, and QKFormer has its particularities, i.e., 1) it achieved **SOTA** performance on ImageNet, and 2) it adopts **a unique hierarchical mechanism**, we specifically focused on it for our ImageNet experiments[4].

## Response to Gap Between Original Paper & Results
Currently, the related works on Spiking Transformer use different approaches for model construction and performance evaluation (such as employing different data augmentations and training scripts), resulting in a lack of fair comparisons. Our goal is to provide **a unified, reproducible, and scalable benchmarking platform** to fill this gap. Therefore, in our framework, all models are trained using the same setup, and no cherry-picking is done to ensure fairness in the comparison. Since the setup used in our work differs from that of previous works, there will be discrepancies in the results.

## Response to Surrogate Gradient Study
Thank you for your valuable suggestion. Due to the unique structure and dynamics of SNNs, surrogate gradients are required to enable effective backpropagation and weight updates. The choice of surrogate gradient functions, as well as the associated internal parameters, serve as important hyperparameters. Following your suggestion, we applied different surrogate gradients and hyperparameter settings (specifically, the alpha parameter) to the three representative models. This was done to evaluate whether the STEP framework and Spiking Transformer can maintain robustness across varying settings.

We thank the reviewer for their careful reading, constructive feedback, and thoughtful suggestions. We address each of the raised concerns below.

## On the Lack of New Benchmark Datasets
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. While the primary objective of STEP is to unify evaluation protocols across existing Spiking Transformer implementations, we fully agree that developing new benchmark datasets is critical for further advancing the field. STEP currently **focuses on establishing a reproducible and standardized evaluation pipeline** across diverse architectures and datasets, which lays a solid foundation for subsequent benchmarking research.
However, as highlighted in our experimental analysis, both static and event-based datasets used in prior works may fall short in revealing the true strengths of Spiking Transformers. In future work, **we plan to design and release more challenging benchmark datasets** that are better aligned with the architectural characteristics of Spiking Transformers, enabling more effective evaluation of their temporal modeling and event-driven computation capabilities.


## On the Limited Scope of Event-based Evaluations and Lack of Comparison with Spiking Object Detection Models
We fully agree with the reviewer that expanding STEP beyond classification is essential for evaluating the full potential of Spiking Transformers. Currently, in addition to traditional classification tasks (such as CIFAR10/100, ImageNet), the framework also supports **event classification** tasks (such as CIFAR10-DVS), **sequence classification** tasks (sCIFAR, sMNIST), **audio classification** tasks (SHD), **segmentation** tasks (ADE20K), **detection** tasks (COCO), and **3D point cloud** tasks (ModelNet10/40, ScanObjectNN). The framework will also gradually adapt to event-based segmentation and detection tasks. In addition, the capabilities of STEP are not limited to Transformer-based models. ## On the Validity of Energy Modeling without Real Hardware Measurements
We appreciate the reviewer’s emphasis on the importance of energy evaluation in benchmarking spiking models. We would like to clarify that our energy estimation goes beyond conventional AC/MAC counting: our framework is **the first to incorporate both compute and memory access energy when evaluating Spiking Transformers**. This is a significant advancement over prior work, which typically overlooks memory energy despite its considerable contribution to total energy consumption—especially in attention-based architectures with high memory bandwidth demands.
Regarding the use of simulation rather than physical measurement on neuromorphic chips, we must highlight a practical constraint: current neuromorphic hardware (e.g., TrueNorth, Loihi) does not support Spiking Transformers due to their reliance on operations incompatible with event-driven execution (e.g., softmax attention, layer normalization). Even if compatibility existed, deploying a model like Spike-driven Transformer 8-512 (with 12950016 neurons) on Loihi (130000 neurons per chip) would require over 100 chips, which is **far beyond the hardware scale** of most practical benchmarks. Hence, analytical and simulation-based estimation remains the most feasible and generalizable approach at this stage of research.

## Response to Theoretical Analysis and Potential Applications
Spiking Transformers have shown strong potential in the SNN domain due to their sparse, event-driven computations and energy-efficient characteristics. These properties make them **promising for deployment in neuromorphic hardware and low-power edge AI systems**, particularly for 3D data and event-based visual perception[1]. We will include a discussion on such applications **in the final version** to contextualize the relevance of our work.

While STEP primarily aims to standardize fragmented evaluation practices, we also partially address the theoretical interaction between spiking dynamics and attention mechanisms. We analyze the design mechanism of spiking attention, where the use of matrix multiplication to replace Softmax and the resulting reduced attention complexity could significantly compromise the ability of the attention mechanism to capture global features[2][3]. From this perspective,  Section 5 provides **extensive component-level analyses**, such as randomized attention and convolution depth ablations, which **suggest that current spike-based attention modules contribute only marginally to performance**. Convolutional frontends remain the dominant contributors. Our analysis offers high-level guidance for the future development of Spiking Transformers. Rather than mimicking ANN-style depth and parameter stacking, we suggest that future designs may benefit from more brain-inspired mechanisms—such as biologically plausible neurons and temporally structured attention.

The paper presents STEP , a new framework designed to evaluate Spiking Transformers—models that aim to merge the efficiency of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) with the powerful attention mechanisms of traditional Transformers. The main contributions of this work are:
1. Creating a centralized platform that brings together various implementations of Spiking Transformers for fair and reproducible comparisons.
2. Supporting multiple tasks (classification, segmentation, detection), datasets (static, event-based, sequential), and framework backends (e.g., SpikingJelly, BrainCog, BrainPy).
3. Conducting detailed ablation studies to understand how different components—like neuron types, encoding methods, and attention modules—affect performance.
4. Introducing an energy consumption estimation model, which challenges some common assumptions about the energy benefits of SNNs over conventional models.
5. Offering insights into current limitations of Spiking Transformers and suggesting directions for future research.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This is one of the first attempts to bring consistency to the evaluation of Spiking Transformers, an area that’s gaining momentum. With inconsistent practices across papers, this kind of standardized benchmarking fills a real gap in the field.
2. The authors run extensive experiments on diverse datasets and architectures. Their ablation studies offer valuable insights into what works—and what doesn’t—when building spiking versions of Transformers.
3. The code is publicly available and well-documented, which is essential for reproducibility. Its modular design makes it easy for others to build upon or adapt to their own use cases.
4. Beyond just benchmarking, the paper includes a critical discussion of current shortcomings in Spiking Transformers. The energy analysis, in particular, adds nuance to the ongoing debate around the efficiency of SNNs versus quantized ANNs.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. As a benchmarking platform, the paper is naturally more focused on engineering and evaluation than on theoretical innovation. While understandable, it would have been interesting to see some principled analysis of how attention and spiking dynamics interact.
2. Due to computational limits, not all existing Spiking Transformer variants could be evaluated. The authors acknowledge this, but it might be helpful to suggest ways the community can extend the framework to include more models in the future.
3. Most results are presented without confidence intervals or standard deviation. This is fairly common in benchmarking papers, but including such details could make the conclusions more robust.
4. The paper states there are no direct societal impacts, but a short discussion of potential applications—like edge AI or neuromorphic computing—would help situate the work within a larger context.

summary.value: This paper introduces STEP, a unified benchmarking framework designed to standardize the evaluation of Spiking Transformers across different architectures, datasets, and tasks. STEP consolidates diverse implementations into a consistent pipeline, supporting classification, segmentation, and detection tasks on both static and event-based datasets. Through extensive experiments, we reproduce and compare multiple representative models, finding that current Spiking Transformers still depend heavily on convolutional preprocessing—while gaining only limited benefits from attention mechanisms. Our framework provides a foundation for developing more efficient, robust, and biologically grounded spike-native Transformers in future research.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The authors for their comprehensive experiments spanning multiple tasks and datasets - this represents an impressive amount of rigorous work.

2. The writing is good, technically precise yet remarkably clear and readable, with truly polished language.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. While the authors provide thorough performance evaluations across multiple tasks, the work does not introduce new datasets. From a dataset and benchmarking perspective, this somewhat limits the scope of contribution to the field. Future work could consider developing novel benchmark datasets to further advance the domain.

2. The STEP framework shows promising results on event-based vision datasets, though currently focused primarily on classification tasks. To strengthen the work, I recommend extending evaluations to: high-level event-based tasks (e.g., object detection on PKU-DAVIS-SOD [1]), and comparative analysis with spiking CNN approaches (e.g., EMS-YOLO [2]). This expansion would provide more comprehensive insights into the framework's capabilities across different architectures and task complexities.

[1] Sodformer: Streaming object detection with transformer using events and frames, TPAMI 2023.

[2] Deep directly-trained spiking neural networks for object detection, ICCV 2023.

3. As a benchmark, the evaluation methodology is crucial for the future of this field. The authors assess the energy efficiency of SNNs primarily using conventional simulation methods (calculating AC/MAC energy consumption) rather than actual testing on neuromorphic chips. This raises some concerns for me: Is this approach truly valid? Please explain the rationale and suggest better alternatives.

summary.value: This paper presents the first benchmarking framework for Spiking Transformers, integrating several representative architectures. It is the first to unify classification, segmentation, and detection tasks within a single evaluation platform and supports a diverse range of datasets—greatly facilitating the development and assessment of Spiking Transformers. The authors conduct systematic experiments involving multiple input encoding schemes, spiking neuron types, and attention mechanisms. Based on these experiments, the paper identifies common limitations in current Spiking Transformers and provides valuable insights for future architectural improvements.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This is the first comprehensive benchmarking framework tailored for Spiking Transformers, supporting multi-task and multi-dataset evaluation.
2. The framework enables consistent comparisons by integrating multiple spiking neuron models and representative architectures.
3. It conducts detailed horizontal and vertical comparisons across input encodings, neuron types, embedding strategies, and attention mechanisms.
4. The study identifies important limitations in current designs: (1) redundancy in attention mechanisms; (2) excessive dependence on complex embedding frontends.
5. Overall, the framework establishes a strong baseline for future work in Spiking Transformer development and offers practical suggestions for optimization.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Why did the authors use different representative models for ImageNet and other datasets instead of evaluating a consistent set of models across all benchmarks?
2. Several reproduced results differ from those reported in the original papers. What could be the reasons behind these discrepancies?
3. While the paper explores the impact of neurons, encodings, and attention modules, it overlooks the potential influence of surrogate gradient choices (e.g., function type, scaling factor). A brief discussion or experiment would improve completeness.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: Thanks to the authors for the detailed response and my questions have been addressed. I do not have further questions and keep my original rating.

summary.value: This paper presents STEP, a unified benchmark framework designed to standardize the evaluation and development of Spiking Transformers. Aiming to address the current fragmentation in implementations and experimental setups, STEP supports a broad spectrum of tasks—including classification, segmentation, and detection—across static, event-based, and sequential datasets. The framework offers modular components for spiking neurons, input encodings, surrogate gradients, and supports multiple backends such as SpikingJelly and BrainCog. Through extensive reproducibility efforts and ablation studies, the paper provides insights into key architectural choices and proposes a unified energy estimation model. Findings reveal that current Spiking Transformers heavily depend on convolutional frontends and lack robust temporal modeling, highlighting the need for spike-native design innovations.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This paper introduces STEP, a comprehensive and well-structured benchmarking framework that unifies the evaluation of Spiking Transformers across multiple tasks and data modalities. Its modular design and support for various backends (e.g., SpikingJelly, BrainCog) significantly lower the barrier to reproducibility and fair comparison in this emerging field.

2. The authors conduct extensive and systematic experiments, including reproduction of representative models and detailed ablation studies. These analyses yield valuable insights into the influence of architectural components—such as spiking neuron types and input encoding—on performance, shedding light on important design factors that are often overlooked.

3. By proposing a unified analytical model for energy estimation that accounts for spike sparsity, bitwidth, and memory access, the paper provides a more realistic and nuanced view of energy efficiency. This challenges previous assumptions and encourages more rigorous benchmarking between SNNs and quantized ANNs, contributing to a more grounded understanding of practical deployment trade-offs.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. This paper focuses solely on unifying benchmarks for Spiking Transformers, which raises questions about why the scope does not extend to all spiking neural network architectures. The framework’s limited focus may restrict its broader applicability and impact within the spiking neural network community.

2. The authors do not sufficiently discuss whether the proposed unified evaluation standards ensure fair comparisons across different models. Further elaboration on the rationale, limitations, and fairness of these standards would strengthen the credibility of the benchmarking results.

3. Although the unified energy estimation model is a valuable contribution, its accuracy and generalizability rely heavily on assumptions about hardware factors such as memory access costs and spike sparsity. The lack of validation on real-world hardware or deployment scenarios may limit confidence in the reported energy efficiency comparisons.

title.value: STEP: A Unified Spiking Transformer Evaluation Platform for Fair and Reproducible Benchmarking

abstract.value: Spiking Transformers have recently emerged as promising architectures for combining the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the representational power of self-attention. However, the lack of standardized implementations, evaluation pipelines, and consistent design choices has hindered fair comparison and principled analysis. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{STEP}, a unified benchmark framework for Spiking Transformers that supports a wide range of tasks, including classification, segmentation, and detection across static, event-based, and sequential datasets. STEP provides modular support for diverse components such as spiking neurons, input encodings, surrogate gradients, and multiple backends (e.g., SpikingJelly, BrainCog). Using STEP, we reproduce and evaluate several representative models, and conduct systematic ablation studies on attention design, neuron types, encoding schemes, and temporal modeling capabilities. We also propose a unified analytical model for energy estimation, accounting for spike sparsity, bitwidth, and memory access, and show that quantized ANNs may offer comparable or better energy efficiency. Our results suggest that current Spiking Transformers rely heavily on convolutional frontends and lack strong temporal modeling, underscoring the need for spike-native architectural innovations.  The full code is available at: https://github.com/Fancyssc/STEP.
